questions.question: An IS auditor finds that a release's source code is baselined, but its approved design specifications can be edited freely. Which conclusion is MOST appropriate?

options.A: Specification edits are traceable through the tool's version history
options.B: The specifications should be configuration items in the baseline
options.C: The specifications should be locked against editing by the design lead
options.D: Specification edits are acceptable if rebaselined at the next release review

questions.key_concept: Configuration items include code, designs, requirements and builds; all must be under formal change control as part of the baseline.
questions.pre_read: Ask what belongs in a product baseline. Then ask how approved changes to it should happen.
questions.correct_explanation: A configuration item is any identified artifact placed under formal change control as part of the product baseline, including requirements, designs, code and build files. Uncontrolled specifications mean the baseline cannot be trusted. A read-only lock is the tempting option: it stops unauthorized edits, but it gives approved changes no controlled path and rests on one person instead of a change process.

wrong_explanations.A: Version history shows who edited what, but no one authorizes the edit; traceability after the fact is not change control.
wrong_explanations.C: A lock stops edits, but it offers no way to authorize, record and baseline the changes the project will still need, and it relies on one person.
wrong_explanations.D: Rebaselining later records edits after they happen; configuration management requires authorization before a baselined item changes.

tips: Eliminate: A treats an edit history as control although nothing authorizes the edits, and D reviews edits after the fact, which detects rather than prevents.
Final two: B beats C because configuration management blocks unauthorized edits and gives approved changes a controlled path; a lock only blocks.
Exam cue: a configuration item is any controlled artifact in the baseline, not just code, and not just hardware.

questions.question: An IS auditor must confirm that customer balances migrated completely and accurately to a new core platform. Which evidence is BEST?

options.A: User acceptance test results for the main workflows
options.B: Record counts and control totals reconciled source to target
options.C: A sample of accounts compared on screen in both systems
options.D: Conversion logs showing each record was read and written

questions.key_concept: Data conversion integrity is evidenced by source-to-target reconciliation of record counts and control totals, with variances investigated.
questions.pre_read: Focus on the words completely and accurately. Ask which evidence compares the data itself, not the system's behavior.
questions.correct_explanation: Completeness and accuracy of converted data are proven by reconciling source and target in full: matching record counts, control totals and hash totals, with every variance investigated. Comparing a sample of accounts on screen is the tempting option because it examines the data itself, but a sample cannot prove that every balance arrived, so missing or altered records outside it go undetected.

wrong_explanations.A: Acceptance testing checks that workflows function. It does not prove that every migrated record and amount matches the source.
wrong_explanations.C: A sample checks some accounts in detail but cannot show that every record and balance transferred.
wrong_explanations.D: The conversion program's logs report its own activity; they count records handled but cannot show balances arrived unaltered, which needs reconciled control totals.

tips: Eliminate: A tests workflows rather than the migrated data, and D relies on the conversion program's own record counts, which say nothing about amounts.
Final two: B beats C because full reconciliation covers every record and total; a sample cannot prove completeness.
Exam cue: for data conversion, completeness and accuracy evidence means counts and control totals matched between source and target.

questions.question: An IS auditor finds that several failed production changes were approved by a change advisory board (CAB) that checks only each change's description and timing. What should the auditor recommend as MOST effective?

options.A: Route standard, normal and emergency changes to the full board
options.B: Require each change to name a business owner who confirms its timing
options.C: Have the board judge readiness from test and backout evidence
options.D: Hold a post-implementation review of each failed change

questions.key_concept: A change advisory board assesses the risk, impact and readiness of significant changes before authorization; it neither plans nor executes them.
questions.pre_read: Separate who sits on a board from what it checks. Then ask whether each fix acts before or after a change.
questions.correct_explanation: A CAB adds value by assessing the risk, test evidence and backout plan of significant changes before authorizing them; approving on description and timing alone lets untested or unrecoverable changes through. A post-implementation review of failures is the tempting option: it captures lessons, but it acts after the damage and does not stop the next weak change from being approved.

wrong_explanations.A: Standard changes are pre-authorized and emergency changes follow an expedited path reviewed soon after; routing them all to the full board adds volume without deepening the check on risky ones.
wrong_explanations.B: A business owner confirming timing adds accountability for when a change runs, but the board would still not assess its risk, testing or backout plan.
wrong_explanations.D: Reviewing failures afterward supports learning, but it is detective; the board's main value is assessment before authorization.

tips: Eliminate: A floods the full board with pre-authorized standard and urgent emergency changes, and B adds an owner who confirms timing, which the board already checks.
Final two: C beats D because a CAB adds most assurance by assessing risk before authorization; reviewing failures afterward is detective.
Exam cue: change governance assures by checking risk, testing and backout before approval; pick the fix that strengthens the pre-approval check.

questions.question: An organization is buying business-critical custom software from a small start-up vendor. Which contract provision should the IS auditor MOST recommend?

options.A: Source code escrow with defined release conditions
options.B: A right-to-audit clause over the vendor's development process
options.C: A performance bond payable if the vendor fails to deliver
options.D: Financial backing from the vendor's parent company if the vendor defaults

questions.key_concept: Source code escrow protects continuity of business-critical custom software when the vendor may fail or stop supporting it.
questions.pre_read: Identify the main risk: the vendor might not survive. Ask which provision still works after the vendor is gone.
questions.correct_explanation: Escrow places the source code with an independent agent and releases it if defined events occur, such as vendor failure. For business-critical custom software from a vendor whose survival is uncertain, that protects continuity. A right-to-audit clause is the strongest alternative: it gives visibility into how the vendor builds software, but it does nothing if the vendor stops trading.

wrong_explanations.B: Audit rights help assess development quality while the vendor operates. They provide no access to source code if it fails.
wrong_explanations.C: A bond pays compensation, but money does not keep critical software supported once the vendor is gone.
wrong_explanations.D: Parent backing compensates for a default, but it neither supplies the source code nor keeps the software maintainable.

tips: Eliminate: C and D compensate in money, a bond or parent backing, rather than preserving the software itself.
Final two: A beats B because escrow secures source code if the vendor fails; audit rights only give visibility while it operates.
Exam cue: critical custom software plus a fragile single vendor points to escrow with clear release triggers.

questions.question: An IS auditor finds orders reaching processing with customer numbers that match no customer on file. Which control is MOST likely missing?

options.A: A range check on each customer number at entry
options.B: A check digit verified on each customer number at entry
options.C: A format check on each customer number's length and characters
options.D: An existence check against the customer master records

questions.key_concept: Each input edit catches a different defect: check digits catch keying errors, while existence checks confirm a referenced record actually exists.
questions.pre_read: Ask what exactly is wrong with the customer numbers. Then pick the edit that tests that defect.
questions.correct_explanation: A customer number can be in range and carry a valid check digit yet belong to no customer. Only an existence check, a lookup against the customer master records, rejects numbers that match no real customer before processing. The check digit is the tempting option: it catches keying errors such as transposed digits, but a well-formed number that was never issued still passes it.

wrong_explanations.A: A range check confirms the number falls within allowed limits; a number inside the range can still belong to no customer.
wrong_explanations.B: Check digits do stop most mistyped numbers at entry, yet form and existence are separate questions, and each input edit answers only one.
wrong_explanations.C: A format check confirms the number is well formed; a well-formed number can still match no customer on file.

tips: Eliminate: A tests the number's limits and C its format; neither confirms the customer exists.
Final two: D beats B because only a lookup against the master records proves the customer exists; a check digit tests the number's form.
Exam cue: match the edit to the defect: keying errors point to check digits, references to nothing point to existence checks.

questions.question: An IS auditor finds that the feasibility study for a major enterprise resource planning (ERP) investment assesses technical fit and cost-benefit in depth. What should the auditor recommend FIRST?

options.A: Add a sensitivity analysis of the cost and benefit estimates
options.B: Have the ERP vendor confirm the study's technical findings
options.C: Add vendor stability, licensing and ongoing support costs to the study
options.D: Extend the study to operational, legal and schedule feasibility

questions.key_concept: A complete feasibility study covers technical, economic, legal, operational and schedule dimensions before the go/no-go decision.
questions.pre_read: List the feasibility dimensions a go/no-go decision needs. Then check which ones this study covers.
questions.correct_explanation: A go/no-go decision needs every feasibility dimension: technical, economic, operational, legal and schedule. Any one can sink a technically sound, profitable project, so the missing dimensions should be studied before approval. A sensitivity analysis is the tempting option because it makes the economic case more rigorous, but it deepens a dimension already covered and leaves operational, legal and schedule risks unexamined.

wrong_explanations.A: Sensitivity analysis stress-tests the cost and benefit estimates, a dimension already covered; operational, legal and schedule risks stay unexamined.
wrong_explanations.B: A vendor's confirmation is not independent, and technical fit is the dimension the study already covers in depth.
wrong_explanations.C: Licensing and support costs belong to the economic dimension the study already covers, and vendor stability is a supplier-selection check; operational, legal and schedule feasibility stay unexamined.

tips: Eliminate: B relies on the vendor to confirm a dimension already covered, and C adds costs the economic study covers plus a supplier-selection check, not a missing dimension.
Final two: D beats A because the gap is missing dimensions; a sensitivity analysis only stress-tests the economic case already studied.
Exam cue: close feasibility gaps before approval, and remember TELOS: technical, economic, legal, operational, schedule.

questions.question: An IS auditor finds that a support team's urgent fixes either wait for the next two-week sprint or skip sprint planning. Which delivery method should the auditor consider the MOST suitable fit?

options.A: Scrum, adding each urgent fix to the current sprint on arrival
options.B: Kanban, with work-in-progress limits and pull-based flow
options.C: Scrum, with shorter one-week sprints and sprint commitments
options.D: Waterfall releases, with an emergency change path for urgent fixes

questions.key_concept: Kanban fits continuous, variable-priority work through pull-based flow and WIP limits; Scrum fits time-boxed iterative product development.
questions.pre_read: Look at how the work arrives and what happens to urgent items. Ask which method keeps them inside the process.
questions.correct_explanation: Kanban suits work that arrives continuously: items are pulled when capacity frees up, so urgent fixes enter the process instead of waiting or going around it, and work-in-progress limits keep the flow controlled. Shorter sprints are the tempting option, but they still batch work into fixed commitments, so an urgent fix must still wait days or break the sprint.

wrong_explanations.A: Adding fixes mid-sprint breaks the sprint commitment each time and turns the current bypass of sprint planning into policy.
wrong_explanations.C: Shorter sprints would win if urgent fixes could wait a few days; a delivery method follows the shape of demand, not the planning calendar.
wrong_explanations.D: Emergency change is meant for genuine emergencies; sending routine support work through it overloads that path and weakens control, while releases still batch other work.

tips: Eliminate: A breaks the sprint commitment whenever a fix arrives, and D sends routine support work through the emergency path meant for true emergencies.
Final two: B beats C because pull-based flow lets urgent work enter the process; shorter sprints still batch work into commitments.
Exam cue: continuous, interrupt-driven work points to Kanban; when urgent work goes around a process, fix the fit so it stays inside the control.

questions.question: A QA manager reports 95 percent code coverage on a payments module, yet defects keep reaching production. Which evidence would BEST show the IS auditor how effective the test suite is?

options.A: A coverage report showing 100 percent of statements executed by tests
options.B: A count of automated tests passing on each build
options.C: A count of defects found in system testing before release
options.D: A mutation score showing how many seeded faults the tests detect

questions.key_concept: Mutation testing measures test-suite effectiveness by checking whether tests catch deliberately injected faults; coverage only shows what code ran.
questions.pre_read: Separate 'code was executed' from 'a fault would be detected'. Ask which technique measures the second.
questions.correct_explanation: A mutation score measures effectiveness directly: small faults are seeded into the code, and the share the tests catch shows whether they check results. Full statement coverage is the tempting option, but coverage only shows which lines ran; tests can execute every line with weak assertions, which is exactly why defects escape despite 95 percent coverage.

wrong_explanations.A: More coverage shows more lines executed, not that tests check results; high coverage with weak assertions already explains the escapes.
wrong_explanations.B: A passing count shows activity, not strength; weak tests pass easily, so green builds can coexist with escaping defects.
wrong_explanations.C: Defect counts depend on code quality and tester effort; a low count cannot show whether the automated suite would catch faults.

tips: Eliminate: B counts tests that pass, which weak tests do easily, and C counts defects, which depends on code quality, not test strength.
Final two: D beats A because mutation scores show whether tests catch faults, while coverage only shows which lines ran.
Exam cue: high coverage plus escaped defects signals weak assertions; mutation testing measures what the tests actually verify.

questions.question: Halfway through the quarter, a customer-facing service with an agreed error-budget policy has used its entire error budget. Which release response should the IS auditor expect management to take FIRST?

options.A: Re-measure the SLO over a longer window before changing releases
options.B: Freeze non-essential releases and prioritize reliability work
options.C: Keep releasing, using canary rollouts and extra production monitoring
options.D: Add on-call engineers and continue the planned release schedule

questions.key_concept: When an error budget is exhausted, non-essential releases stop and reliability work takes priority until the budget recovers.
questions.pre_read: Recall what an error budget is for: it decides when the team may keep shipping features and when it must stop.
questions.correct_explanation: An exhausted error budget means users have already absorbed the agreed amount of unreliability. The agreed policy response is to freeze non-essential changes and spend engineering effort on reliability until the budget recovers. Canary rollouts with extra monitoring reduce the risk of each release, but they still spend reliability the service no longer has and sidestep the agreed policy.

wrong_explanations.A: A longer window can look like better analysis, but changing how the SLO is measured after the budget runs out delays the agreed response and hides the reliability problem.
wrong_explanations.C: Safer rollout methods reduce per-release risk but still add change to a service that has used up its tolerance for failure.
wrong_explanations.D: Extra on-call staff speed recovery from failures, but the agreed policy pauses non-essential change once the budget is spent; releasing on schedule keeps spending reliability already used up.

tips: Eliminate: A and D, because A changes how the SLO is measured after the budget runs out, and D keeps the release schedule that the agreed policy pauses.
Final two: B beats C because the policy for an exhausted budget is to stop non-essential change, not to release more carefully.
Exam cue: once the error budget is spent, feature releases pause and reliability work takes priority until it recovers.

questions.question: At month 8 of a 14-month ERP project, the PMO reports a cumulative CPI of 0.78 and SPI of 0.85; the team says recent rebaselining will fix this. What should the IS auditor conclude FIRST?

options.A: Performance is within tolerance for a complex ERP rollout
options.B: A conclusion should wait until rebaselined figures mature
options.C: Earned value analysis cannot yet predict outcomes at this stage
options.D: Cost and schedule are materially behind and need corrective action

questions.key_concept: Cumulative CPI and SPI well below 1.0 at mid-project signal material variance that rarely self-corrects and needs corrective action.
questions.pre_read: CPI (cost performance index) and SPI (schedule performance index) compare earned value with actual cost and planned value; below 1.0 means behind.
questions.correct_explanation: Cumulative indices of 0.78 and 0.85 at month 8 mean the project earns 78 cents of value per dollar spent and is 15% behind plan; cumulative CPI rarely recovers much after mid-project. The auditor should report a material variance needing action. Waiting for rebaselined data sounds prudent, but rebaselining resets the yardstick without fixing performance and delays the decision.

wrong_explanations.A: A CPI of 0.78 is well below accepted tolerance. Calling it normal for ERP hides a material overrun.
wrong_explanations.B: Rebaselining changes the plan, not the performance. Waiting delays corrective action while costs keep overrunning.
wrong_explanations.C: By mid-project, cumulative earned value indices are reliable predictors; cumulative CPI tends to stabilize early.

tips: Eliminate: A treats earning only 78 cents of value per dollar spent as normal, and C wrongly claims earned value analysis cannot predict at mid-project.
Final two: D beats B because rebaselining resets the yardstick but does not fix performance; waiting only delays corrective action.
Exam cue: CPI or SPI well below 1.0 past the midpoint signals real variance; a rebaseline resets the plan, never the performance, so it cannot explain variance away.

questions.question: A fraud-detection model's false-positive rate has risen from 4% to 11% in eight months; its go-live plan did not cover monitoring. What should the IS auditor recommend as the BEST response?

options.A: Retrain the model on the most recent eight months of data
options.B: Raise the alert threshold and monitor false positives weekly
options.C: Put the model under lifecycle governance with drift thresholds
options.D: Assign an independent validation team to revalidate the model now

questions.key_concept: Production ML needs lifecycle governance: an accountable owner, drift monitoring, retraining triggers and performance gates.
questions.pre_read: Separate the symptom (rising errors) from the cause. Ask why the decline went unmanaged for eight months.
questions.correct_explanation: The rising false-positive rate is a symptom; the root cause is that monitoring was never planned, so drift (accuracy falling as real data changes) went unaddressed for eight months. Lifecycle governance, with an accountable owner, drift thresholds and retraining triggers, keeps the model reliable over time. An independent revalidation is the tempting option, but it checks only today's model; revalidation belongs inside the lifecycle.

wrong_explanations.A: Retraining may correct today's drift, but an unvalidated retrained model is an uncontrolled change, and with no monitoring in place the next drift goes unnoticed.
wrong_explanations.B: A higher threshold cuts false positives but lets more fraud through; watching the rate weekly does not address why the model drifts.
wrong_explanations.D: Revalidation checks today's model, but without ongoing monitoring, drift thresholds or retraining triggers, the next degradation would again go unmanaged.

tips: Eliminate: A retrains and redeploys without validation, itself an uncontrolled model change, and B trades false positives for missed fraud.
Final two: C beats D because governance keeps catching drift as it happens, while a one-time revalidation only checks today's model.
Exam cue: when a symptom comes with a missing control framework, recommend the framework, not the one-time fix.

tips: Eliminate: A places security testing after acceptance, when it belongs before go-live, and D treats warranty support as project work instead of an operational or contract activity.

questions.question: An IS auditor reviews the reconciliation tolerances proposed to decide cutover after a parallel run. Which basis for the tolerances should the auditor consider BEST?

options.B: One materiality threshold for balances, rates and reference data
options.C: Tolerances the migration vendor used on its past projects
options.D: Per-category thresholds based on materiality and business impact

questions.key_concept: Parallel-run reconciliation tolerances should be set per data category by materiality and business impact, with documented investigation rules.
questions.pre_read: Notice the stem asks for a basis for tolerances. Ask which option ties acceptable variance to the impact of the error.
questions.correct_explanation: Tolerances should be risk-based: financial balances may need near-zero variance, while descriptive reference fields can tolerate more, each with documented investigation rules. This focuses effort where an error would matter. Zero tolerance sounds rigorous, but it treats a trivial formatting difference like a misstated balance, consumes investigation effort on immaterial items and can delay cutover without reducing meaningful risk.

wrong_explanations.A: Zero tolerance is defensible for cash balances, yet a threshold exists to sort errors that matter from noise, and one that sorts nothing is no threshold.
wrong_explanations.B: One threshold for every category treats balances and reference fields alike, though materiality differs by data category and business impact.
wrong_explanations.C: Another project's tolerances reflect different data and risks; they are not tied to the materiality of this organization's categories.

tips: Eliminate: B applies one threshold across categories whose materiality differs, and C borrows tolerances set for other organizations' data.
Final two: D beats A because materiality-based thresholds focus scrutiny where errors matter, while zero tolerance spends it everywhere equally.
Exam cue: when a threshold must be set, prefer risk-based and materiality-driven over uniform or absolute rules.

options.B: Run both core platforms in parallel until migration completes
options.C: Migrate shared infrastructure first, then customer-facing systems
options.D: Migrate the highest-risk systems first to retire risk early

questions.key_concept: M&A IT integration should discover the acquired systems and dependencies first, then sequence migrations by risk.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the acquirer does not yet know about the acquired bank, and what must happen before migrations are ordered.
questions.correct_explanation: An acquired bank's real environment rarely matches its documentation: integrations, custom rules and in-flight projects must be discovered before migration is planned. Moving shared infrastructure first sounds dependency-aware, but it fixes the order before the acquired bank's real links are known.

wrong_explanations.B: Running both platforms for the whole program doubles operating cost and reconciliation effort, and it does not decide what moves when.
wrong_explanations.C: An infrastructure-first order is a common migration pattern, but patterns from other estates stay hypotheses until this estate's dependencies are mapped.
wrong_explanations.D: Moving the riskiest systems first sounds prudent, but risk cannot be ranked before dependencies are discovered, and failures would hit the most critical systems first.

tips: Eliminate: B runs two platforms for the whole program without ordering the moves, and D sends the highest-risk systems through a migration process not yet proven on anything.
Final two: A beats C because the order must follow dependencies discovered in the acquired bank, not a fixed rule set before discovery.

questions.question: An IS auditor finds that a nine-hour regression suite, made up mostly of end-to-end UI tests, is often skipped before urgent releases. What should the auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Rebalance to equal numbers of unit, integration and end-to-end tests
options.B: Run the suite in parallel across more build agents
options.C: Run the full suite weekly instead of before each release
options.D: Rebalance toward many fast unit tests and few end-to-end tests

questions.key_concept: The test pyramid favors many fast unit tests, fewer integration tests and the fewest end-to-end tests for cost-effective coverage.
questions.pre_read: Ask why the suite is skipped. Then pick the change that removes that cause without leaving releases untested.
questions.correct_explanation: The suite is skipped because it is slow, so the fix is its composition: the test pyramid puts many fast unit tests at the base, fewer integration tests and few end-to-end tests, kept for critical business flows so coverage is kept. That gives quick feedback teams will not bypass. Running the suite in parallel is the tempting option because it cuts run time quickly, but the slow, brittle tests remain.

wrong_explanations.A: Equal counts keep many slow end-to-end tests, so run times stay long and the pressure to skip the suite remains.
wrong_explanations.B: More agents shorten the run at extra cost, but the suite stays dominated by slow end-to-end tests, so run times and cost grow again as it expands.
wrong_explanations.C: A weekly run avoids the delay but lets urgent releases ship without regression testing, which is the risk itself.

tips: Eliminate: A keeps many slow end-to-end tests by counting layers equally, and C removes the delay by leaving releases untested.
Final two: D beats B because a pyramid shortens the suite at its root; more agents buy speed with cost while the slow tests remain.
Exam cue: when a control is skipped because it is slow, fix its design so it fits the process; for regression suites, think pyramid.

questions.question: A project team is defining security controls for a new patient-records application. Which basis should the IS auditor expect as MOST appropriate for deriving the control requirements?

options.C: A risk assessment informed by the data's classification

questions.key_concept: Control requirements come from a risk assessment informed by data classification; frameworks help select controls, not decide what is needed.

Applying a full framework catalog is the most tempting alternative: it looks thorough, but it ignores this system's specific risks, adding unneeded controls and possibly missing context-specific ones.

wrong_explanations.A: Another client's controls reflect that client's risks. They may not fit this application's data, users or threats.
wrong_explanations.B: An auditor would check coverage against a recognized framework, but a catalog lists what is possible; risk decides what is required.
wrong_explanations.D: Budget shapes choices, but letting it define the requirements leaves high risks uncontrolled without a deliberate decision.

tips: Eliminate: A copies another client's risk profile, and D lets cost, not risk, set the requirements.

questions.question: A new claims system will process 50,000 payments a day, and duplicate payment is the key risk. Which control design should the IS auditor consider MOST effective?

options.B: A daily report of possible duplicates for clerks to investigate
options.C: A policy telling staff to check for duplicates before entry
options.D: An automated check that holds payments matching earlier ones

questions.key_concept: For high-volume, well-defined risks, automated preventive controls built into the application beat manual or detective controls.
questions.pre_read: Compare when each control acts: before the money leaves, or after.
questions.correct_explanation: At 50,000 payments a day, an automated preventive control is most effective: a system check that holds payments matching earlier ones stops duplicates before money leaves, consistently and at volume. The daily duplicates report nearly wins: it is a useful detective control, but it finds duplicates after payment and depends on clerks keeping up with a high-volume queue.

wrong_explanations.A: Monthly sampling detects problems weeks later and examines a fraction of payments. Duplicates paid meanwhile must be recovered.
wrong_explanations.B: A duplicates report earns its place when matches are too fuzzy to block; where a rule can be coded, prevention outranks detection.
wrong_explanations.C: A policy relies on every clerk checking by hand. At high volume it is inconsistent and leaves no reliable evidence.

tips: Eliminate: A samples too little too late, and C relies on manual effort at high volume.
Final two: D beats B because preventing a duplicate beats detecting it after the money has gone.
Exam cue: for high-volume, well-defined risks, prefer automated preventive controls built into the application.

questions.question: A query passed load testing on a 12,000-row test table but overloaded production, which holds 180 million rows. Which recommendation should the IS auditor consider BEST?

options.B: Staging with production-scale data volumes and matching database tiers
options.C: Raising the load test's concurrent users to production peak levels
options.D: Load testing against a 1% sample of production data

questions.key_concept: Performance tests are valid evidence only when staging matches production data volume, infrastructure tier and load patterns.
questions.pre_read: Compare the test table size with production, then ask what the test result really proved.
questions.correct_explanation: The test passed because the environment did not resemble production: a tiny data set produced misleading query behavior. Testing is valid evidence only when conditions represent production, so staging needs realistic data volumes and a matching database tier. Expert code review helps, but query performance depends on data volume and execution plans (how the database chooses to run a query) that a reviewer cannot predict from code alone.

wrong_explanations.A: Review can spot obvious inefficiency, but query behavior at scale depends on data volume, which only representative testing reveals.
wrong_explanations.C: More concurrent users tests concurrency, but the failure came from data volume; a 12,000-row table stays unrepresentative.
wrong_explanations.D: A 1% sample is far closer to production than 12,000 rows, but at about 1.8 million rows it still understates the volume that broke the query.

tips: Eliminate: C fixes concurrency when the failure came from data volume, and D scales the data up but still far below production.
Final two: B beats A because test evidence is valid only when conditions match production; review cannot reproduce scale.
Exam cue: when a test passed but production failed, question how representative the test environment was.

questions.question: A bank deploys to production over 30 times a day, and its external auditor says manual change evidence no longer scales. Which recommendation is BEST?

options.A: Generating tamper-evident records linking each deploy to its approval
options.B: Reconciling deploy logs, tickets and approvals each quarter
options.C: Holding a monthly change-board review of a sample of deployments
options.D: Accepting the pipeline's branch-protection settings as evidence of approval

questions.key_concept: High-frequency delivery is auditable when the pipeline generates tamper-evident change evidence linking every deployment to its approval.
questions.pre_read: Ask which option produces reliable evidence for every change at the moment it happens.
questions.correct_explanation: At this volume, evidence must be produced by the pipeline itself. Automated, tamper-evident records that tie each deployment to its approval, build and approver give complete, reliable evidence the external auditor can test. A quarterly reconciliation of every deployment is the tempting option because it is complete, but it is manual and finds unapproved changes months after release.

wrong_explanations.B: A full reconciliation covers every change, but it is manual and quarterly; unapproved deployments run for months, and the manual effort is what no longer scales.
wrong_explanations.C: Sampling after the fact cannot evidence every change, and unauthorized deployments may go undetected for weeks.
wrong_explanations.D: Branch-protection settings show a control is configured, not that every deployment actually went through an approval.

tips: Eliminate: C samples part of the changes weeks later, and D accepts a configured setting as proof that approvals happened.
Final two: A beats B because evidence created as each change deploys is complete and timely; a quarterly reconciliation finds problems months later.
Exam cue: when volume outgrows manual evidence, look for evidence the pipeline creates as each change deploys, not later manual checks.

Passing scenarios therefore show, requirement by requirement, that delivered behavior matches what the business agreed. Post-release sign-off emails are the tempting option: they show business approval, but they are informal, come after go-live and do not tie approval to specific tested behavior.

wrong_explanations.D: An auditor would keep the emails as corroboration of business satisfaction, but satisfaction is not conformance: requirements are proven criterion by criterion.

questions.pre_read: Ask who benefits if the review finds the project a success, then ask whether that person should write the verdict.
questions.correct_explanation: A post-implementation review must give the sponsor an objective view of whether the system delivered what was promised. A project manager reviewing their own delivery faces a self-review threat and an incentive to present results favorably, so an independent party should lead it. A process-heavy focus is the closest concern: it is a real scoping risk, but it is a symptom of the missing independence, not the root concern.

wrong_explanations.A: A narrow focus on delivery process is a scoping weakness, but it stems from the reviewer's conflict of interest, which is the root concern.
wrong_explanations.B: Relying on status reports is a real evidence weakness, but it follows from who leads the review; the root concern is self-review.
wrong_explanations.C: Business knowledge can be added through sponsors and users; a competence gap is fixable, while judging one's own work undermines every conclusion.

tips: Eliminate: B is an evidence choice an independent reviewer would correct, and C is a competence gap that business participants can fill.
Final two: D beats A because a self-review threat undermines every conclusion; drift toward process is only a symptom of it.
Exam cue: whoever built it should not be the one to judge it; look for the independence problem before the scope problem.

questions.question: A business case lists benefits such as improved efficiency and better customer experience, stated only in general terms. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST before approval?

options.A: Convert every benefit into a financial value before approval
options.B: Ask IT to measure the benefits once the system is live
options.C: Define measurable targets with a business owner for each benefit
options.D: Approve now and have each benefit owner set targets after go-live

questions.key_concept: Every promised benefit needs a measurable target, a baseline and a named business owner before the investment is approved.
questions.pre_read: Ask how anyone could later prove these benefits arrived, and who would answer if they did not.
questions.correct_explanation: Benefits stated in general terms cannot be measured or managed, so the case should give each benefit a measurable target, a baseline and a named business owner accountable for realizing it. Converting every benefit into money is the tempting option: it looks rigorous, but non-financial benefits can be measured without a price, and a valuation with no owner leaves no one accountable for delivering it.

wrong_explanations.A: An auditor would accept money values where conversion is reliable, but a figure's precision never substitutes for someone answering for it.
wrong_explanations.B: IT can supply measurements, but business owners are accountable for benefits, and undefined benefits give nothing to measure.
wrong_explanations.D: Setting targets after go-live lets the review measure whatever happened; even with named owners, targets must be set before approval.

questions.question: After $14M and four months, a new CRM module has won 23 of its 150 target customers. Which advice from the IS auditor to the board is MOST appropriate?

options.B: Continue, but rebaseline the target at 50 customers
options.C: Weigh forward costs and benefits against the alternatives
options.D: Weigh total cost to date and future benefits against alternatives

questions.key_concept: Investment continue-or-stop decisions compare forward costs and benefits against alternatives and exclude sunk cost.

questions.correct_explanation: Money already spent cannot be recovered whichever way the board decides, so it must not drive the choice. tips: Eliminate: A justifies stopping by money already spent, and B moves the target instead of assessing whether further spend is worthwhile.
Final two: C beats D because only future costs and benefits differ between the choices; cost to date is sunk whichever way the board decides.

options.B: Meet the mandated level first, then raise levels by risk
options.C: Pick a mid level matching what peer contractors report
options.D: Reach the mandated level on new releases first, legacy later

questions.key_concept: Assurance targets are set by risk: meet mandatory requirements, then invest in higher maturity where risk reduction justifies the cost, with reassessment gates.
questions.pre_read: Separate what the contract requires now from what risk might justify later.
questions.correct_explanation: A maturity target should first meet the level the contract requires, then rise in phases where the risk reduction justifies the cost, with gates to reassess as requirements evolve. Committing to the top level appears thorough, but it fixes an $8M spend before the firm knows which risks justify it, and it may delay meeting the contract's requirement while the full program is built.

wrong_explanations.A: The top level is a legitimate long-term aim, but compliance sets the floor and risk prices each step above it.
wrong_explanations.C: Copying peers ignores the firm's own contractual floor and risk profile, so the target is neither compliance-based nor risk-based.
wrong_explanations.D: Phasing by release leaves legacy software delivered under the contract below the required level; the contractual minimum applies to every covered product.

tips: Eliminate: C copies peers instead of using the firm's own requirements and risk, and D phases by release, leaving legacy software below the contract's minimum.
Final two: B beats A because investment should follow risk and required compliance, not maximum maturity for its own sake.

questions.question: A post-implementation review cannot confirm a promised 30% cut in claims processing time because nobody recorded processing times before the project. Which IS auditor recommendation BEST addresses the underlying weakness?

options.B: Make a measured starting point a condition of business case approval
options.C: Measure processing times in the new system's reports from now on
options.D: Estimate the baseline from a sample of the archived claim files

questions.key_concept: Benefits can only be proven against a measured starting point, so business cases should record baselines before approval.
questions.pre_read: Separate fixing this one review from fixing the process that let the gap happen.
questions.correct_explanation: The underlying weakness is that the business case was approved without a measured starting point, so no later review can prove the benefit. Making a measured baseline, with an owner and method, a condition of approval fixes this for every future project. Reconstructing the baseline from legacy logs is the tempting option: it may give solid evidence for this review, but it leaves the approval gap in place.

wrong_explanations.A: Legacy logs may rebuild this one baseline, but the approval process that skipped it stays unchanged, so the gap recurs.
wrong_explanations.C: Measuring processing time from now on shows the result, but without a recorded before-figure the 30% cut still cannot be shown, and future projects repeat the gap.
wrong_explanations.D: An estimate from sampled files patches this one review with weaker evidence than full logs, and the approval process that skipped the baseline stays unchanged.

tips: Eliminate: C measures only the after state, so no before-figure exists, and D estimates this one baseline from a sample, leaving the approval gap that caused it.
Final two: B beats A because it fixes the approval process that caused the gap; reconstructing the baseline only patches this one review.
Exam cue: when asked for the fix to an underlying weakness, choose the process change that prevents recurrence, not the one-off workaround.

questions.question: An IS auditor finds that, to meet a regulatory date, a waterfall project plans to deploy to production before system testing is complete. What is the GREATEST risk?

options.A: Defects found after release will cost more to fix in production
options.B: Test documentation will be finished after the system goes live
options.C: The release will go live without a rehearsed rollback
options.D: Unverified code will process live transactions from day one

questions.key_concept: In a waterfall life cycle, system testing gates deployment so unverified code does not reach production and process live transactions.
questions.pre_read: Find which phase gate the plan removes. Ask what that gate exists to prevent.
questions.correct_explanation: In a waterfall life cycle, system testing is the gate that stops unverified code reaching production. Deploying before testing ends removes that gate, so live transactions run on code whose defects have not been found, risking errors in business records. Higher fix costs are the tempting option: they are real, but they are a consequence for IT; the greater risk is to the business processing that relies on the code.

wrong_explanations.A: Late defects do cost more to fix, but that is a cost consequence; the greater risk is untested code processing live business data.
wrong_explanations.B: Late documentation weakens the audit trail, but it does not expose business transactions to undetected defects.
wrong_explanations.C: An unrehearsed rollback weakens recovery, but it matters only after a failure; untested code processing live transactions is the exposure itself.

tips: Eliminate: B is a documentation lag and C weakens recovery after a failure; neither is the exposure the missing test gate creates.
Final two: D beats A because removing the testing gate exposes live business processing; higher fix costs are a consequence for IT.
Exam cue: testing gates deployment; when a plan releases before testing ends, the greatest risk is unverified code in production.

questions.subtopic: Scheduling and the Critical Path. Slippage on a Chain with Slack
questions.question: An IS auditor finds critical-path tasks on schedule, but the data conversion chain, which had five days of total float before go-live, has slipped eight days. What is the MOST LIKELY effect on go-live?

options.A: Go-live holds, because data conversion sits outside the critical path
options.B: Go-live slips eight days, matching the full delay to conversion
options.C: Go-live slips about three days, since conversion now drives the end
options.D: Go-live holds if extra staff join the original critical-path tasks

questions.key_concept: A chain that slips beyond its slack becomes the critical path and moves the end date by the excess.
questions.pre_read: Compare the slip with the slack the chain had before it started to slip.
questions.correct_explanation: Slack, or total float, is how far a chain can slip without moving the end date. The conversion chain had five days, so an eight-day slip uses all of it and adds three more, making conversion the new critical path. Concluding that go-live holds because conversion was not critical comes closest, yet a chain stays non-critical only while its delay stays within its slack.

wrong_explanations.A: Conversion was off the critical path only while its delay stayed within five days of slack; at eight days it drives the end date.
wrong_explanations.B: Five of the eight days are absorbed by the chain's slack, so only the excess three days move go-live.
wrong_explanations.D: The original critical-path tasks are on schedule and no longer the longest chain, so adding staff there cannot pull go-live back.

tips: Eliminate: B counts the full delay although five days of float absorb part of it, and D adds staff to tasks that no longer set the end date.
Final two: C beats A because slack protects a chain only until it is used up; after that, the chain is critical.
Exam cue: subtract the slack from the slip; any excess moves the end date and makes that chain critical.

questions.subtopic: Reverse Engineering. Decompiling Licensed Vendor Software
questions.question: The vendor of a licensed claims-processing engine will not share its design, so developers propose decompiling the engine to build new interfaces. What should the IS auditor recommend FIRST?

options.A: Have legal counsel confirm the decompiling is lawfully permitted
options.B: Request the engine's source code from the software escrow agent
options.C: Carry out the decompiling in an isolated, logged test environment
options.D: Plan integration testing of the new interfaces before go-live

questions.key_concept: A license grants use, not ownership; reverse engineering vendor software needs legal confirmation that the license permits it.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the license actually lets the organization do with the vendor's code.
questions.correct_explanation: A software license grants the right to use the product, not rights to its code. Many licenses forbid decompiling, and many jurisdictions allow it only in narrow cases, such as interoperability, so legal review must come before any work starts. An isolated, logged environment is the strongest alternative: it controls technical risk, such as harm to production, but it does nothing to make the decompiling lawful.

wrong_explanations.B: Escrow releases code only on defined events such as vendor failure; refusing to share design is not one.
wrong_explanations.C: Isolation contains technical risk, but the decompiling itself may breach the license wherever it runs.
wrong_explanations.D: Interface testing is needed later, but it assumes the work behind the interfaces is permitted in the first place.

tips: Eliminate: B relies on escrow, which a design refusal does not trigger, and D is a later step that assumes the work is allowed.
Final two: A beats C because isolation controls technical risk, while the larger risk is legal and arises the moment decompiling starts.
Exam cue: before reverse engineering vendor software, look for legal review of the license terms first.

questions.question: Requirements for a new loan-origination system specify logging of technical errors only, and the project team plans to add business-event logging after go-live. What should the IS auditor consider the GREATEST risk of this plan?

options.A: Adding the logging after go-live will cost more than building it now
options.B: Technical error logs will fill the available storage before testing ends
options.C: Performance tests will not reflect the load of later logging
options.D: Early loan approvals and rate exceptions will have no audit trail

questions.key_concept: Business events must be defined for logging in requirements, because actions taken before logging exists leave no evidence.
questions.pre_read: Ask what happens to accountability for actions taken before the logging is added.
questions.correct_explanation: Business events such as loan approvals and rate exceptions are the evidence of who did what. If they are not logged from go-live, any error or fraud in the early months leaves no trail, and that history can never be recreated. Higher retrofit cost is the closest concern: building controls in early is cheaper, but cost can be absorbed, while missing evidence is lost for good.

wrong_explanations.A: Retrofitting costs more, but the extra cost can be funded later; months of approvals with no record cannot be recovered.
wrong_explanations.B: Storage capacity is a routine operational matter, and nothing suggests error logs will exhaust it.
wrong_explanations.C: The added load can be performance-tested when the logging is added; that is a manageable testing gap, not lost evidence.

tips: Eliminate: B is a routine capacity concern, and C is a testing gap that can be closed when the logging is added.
Final two: D beats A because extra cost can be absorbed, while approvals made without a record leave an evidence gap that can never be filled.
Exam cue: decide which business events to log during design; evidence not captured from day one is gone for good.

questions.question: Business managers will not release staff for requirements workshops on a new claims system, so IT analysts are writing the requirements alone. What should the IS auditor recommend FIRST?

options.A: Proceed, and rely on user acceptance testing to find any gaps
options.B: Escalate to the steering committee to commit knowledgeable users
options.C: Hire external consultants to stand in for the business users
options.D: Have business managers formally sign off the analysts' requirements

questions.key_concept: User management owns requirements and must supply knowledgeable staff; the steering committee resolves gaps in business participation.
questions.pre_read: Ask who can commit business people to the project, and why their input matters.
questions.correct_explanation: User management owns the new system and must supply people who know the work, because requirements written by IT alone often miss how claims are really handled. The steering committee can commit those people, so escalating is the first step. Formal sign-off by business managers is the closest choice: it records ownership, but approving a document they did not help write rarely catches missing needs.

wrong_explanations.A: User acceptance testing finds gaps late, when fixing them means rework; missing needs should be caught while requirements are written.
wrong_explanations.C: Consultants may know the industry but not this organization's claims process, and they cannot take on the business's ownership.
wrong_explanations.D: Sign-off would close the loop if users had helped write the requirements; approval cannot add knowledge that was never gathered.

tips: Eliminate: A finds gaps only after the system is built, and C substitutes outsiders for the business's own knowledge.
Final two: B beats D because sign-off of a document the business did not help write records ownership without supplying its knowledge.
Exam cue: when the business will not take part, escalate; requirements need user ownership, not just user signatures.

questions.subtopic: Purpose and Timing of the Review. Scheduling the First Review
questions.question: A ski resort's new booking system went live in May, and its business case promised faster bookings during the December-to-March season. Which timing for the post-implementation review should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Three months after go-live, as the usual settling interval
options.B: One week after go-live, while the project team is still assembled
options.C: Soon after the first December-to-March period has ended
options.D: After two full booking periods, once planned enhancements are finished

questions.key_concept: Schedule the post-implementation review once the system has run under conditions that let the promised benefits be measured.
questions.pre_read: Ask when the benefit promised in the business case can first be observed.
questions.correct_explanation: A review must wait until the system has run long enough, under representative conditions, to measure the promised benefits. Here the benefit is faster bookings from December to March, so the review belongs soon after the first such period ends, while fixes are still practical. Three months after go-live is the strongest alternative: it is a common settling period, but August data shows off-season volumes and cannot confirm the peak-season benefit.

wrong_explanations.A: An auditor would accept a usual settling interval as a default, but a seasonal promise can only be judged in its season.
wrong_explanations.B: One week after go-live shows start-up problems and the learning curve, not the normal or peak results the review must measure.
wrong_explanations.D: Two booking periods later, context is lost and changes have piled up, so findings come too late to correct cheaply.

tips: Eliminate: B is too early to show anything but start-up issues, and D is too late to act on findings cheaply.
Final two: C beats A because the promised benefit appears only at peak volume, which off-season data cannot show.
Exam cue: time the review for when the promised benefit can actually be measured, not by a fixed number of months.
